dataset: Flame in Freefall - NASA microgravity fire safety findings
notes: Each finding is extracted from the listed NASA source. evidence_type tells whether it is a measured result, an objective, or a hypothesis. safety_score is 1-5 (team judgment) with score_reason.

findings.finding: A large cotton-fiberglass fabric sample (40.6 x 94 cm) burned completely in microgravity with an average flame spread rate of 1.8 mm/s and an estimated flame power of 1200 +/- 300 W.
findings.conditions: Uncrewed Cygnus vehicle after leaving ISS; 20 cm/s concurrent air flow; ~21.5% O2; burn time 420 s
findings.safety_implication: A realistic-size cabin fire can sustain itself and release kilowatt-level heat in microgravity, so it must be detected and fought early.
findings.score_reason: First full-scale spacecraft fire data; directly sets the size of the hazard.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)
source.location: Backup slides: Saffire 1 video summary and Table 1

findings.finding: Flame spread speed was proportional to the air flow velocity: Saffire-I (20 cm/s) burned for about 400 s, Saffire-III (25 cm/s) for about 320 s on the same sample size.
findings.conditions: Large cotton-fiberglass samples, concurrent flow 20 vs 25 cm/s
findings.safety_implication: Cabin ventilation speed directly controls how fast a fire grows; shutting down ventilation is a key first response.
findings.score_reason: Links a controllable spacecraft system (ventilation) to fire growth.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)

findings.finding: Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low gravity reached a steady spread rate, unlike normal gravity where the same samples showed accelerating spread.
findings.conditions: Cotton-fiberglass fabric; concurrent flow
findings.safety_implication: Fire growth models built from Earth tests do not describe spacecraft fires; low-g data is needed for design.
findings.score_reason: Shows Earth intuition about fire growth does not transfer.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)

findings.finding: Concurrent (with-the-wind) flame spread was more sensitive to the flow duct dimensions than previously anticipated.
findings.conditions: Large-scale samples inside the Saffire flow duct
findings.safety_implication: The geometry of the enclosed space (module, rack, duct) changes fire behavior; small-scale tests may underestimate risk.
findings.score_reason: Affects how test results scale to real vehicle volumes.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)

findings.finding: Silicone samples (0.27 to 1.03 mm thick) showed insignificant burning, while 5 cm wide cotton-fiberglass samples burned completely at 2.1 mm/s (20 cm/s flow) and 2.6 mm/s (25 cm/s flow).
findings.conditions: Cygnus vehicle; ~22.1% O2; 5 x 29 cm samples (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 size)
findings.safety_implication: Material choice matters: some cabin materials resist burning in low-g at cabin oxygen, while common fabrics burn fully.
findings.score_reason: Direct material-level comparison under realistic oxygen levels.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)
source.location: Backup Table 1, samples II-1 to II-6

findings.finding: A Nomex fabric sample ignited by a PMMA starter showed essentially no flame spread on the Nomex.
findings.conditions: ~22.1% O2; 20 cm/s concurrent flow
findings.safety_implication: Nomex is a good candidate for cabin fabrics at near-air oxygen levels.
findings.score_reason: Single sample; supports BASS material results.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)

findings.finding: Large-scale fire experiments can be conducted safely inside an uncrewed spacecraft after it leaves the ISS.
findings.conditions: Cygnus resupply vehicles OA-5, OA-6, OA-7 (2016-2017)
findings.safety_implication: Provides a safe way to keep testing realistic fires, detection and cleanup for future vehicles.
findings.score_reason: Methodology, not a direct crew-safety rule.

source.title: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft (Urban et al., NASA GRC, 2017)

findings.finding: Objective: compare low-gravity flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity material screening test using same-size samples (5 x 29 cm).
findings.conditions: 9 samples on one sample card
findings.safety_implication: Tests whether Earth-based material certification is safe enough for space.
findings.score_reason: Objective statement; results are in the Saffire report.

source.title: SAFFIRE-II DoD (PSI-99 Science Documents)

findings.finding: BASS results indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (the standard Earth flammability screening test) is not conservative: materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
findings.conditions: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox; 17 to 21.5% O2; forced air flow
findings.safety_implication: Materials certified as safe on Earth may still burn in a spacecraft; oxygen limits need extra margin.
findings.score_reason: Challenges the main material certification method used for spacecraft.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: Local application of a nitrogen suppressant jet was not adequate to extinguish flames: the jet entrains air and can sustain or even strengthen the flame, even with the ambient airflow turned off.
findings.conditions: Nitrogen jet applied to burning solid samples on ISS
findings.safety_implication: Extinguisher technique from Earth (aim at the base of the flame) may fail or make a fire worse in microgravity.
findings.score_reason: Directly affects how crews should fight fires.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: In opposed flow, flames over thin fabric quickly reached a steady spread rate, and the spread rate was fastest at an intermediate flow speed.
findings.conditions: 2 cm wide cotton-fiberglass fabric; flow stepped from 10 cm/s down to about 1 cm/s
findings.safety_implication: There is a 'worst-case' ventilation speed for fire spread; it should be avoided or accounted for in design.
findings.score_reason: Quantifies how ventilation affects spread.

source.title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (Ferkul et al., 8th US National Combustion Meeting, 2013; PSI-26)

findings.finding: The minimum oxygen needed for flames over solids occurs at a flow speed on the order of 10 cm/s, which also matches the maximum flame spread rate and is typical of spacecraft ventilation.
findings.conditions: Low-speed forced flow in microgravity
findings.safety_implication: Normal spacecraft ventilation speeds are close to the most dangerous condition for fire.
findings.score_reason: Ties the most dangerous condition to everyday cabin operation.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: In concurrent flow, flame spread rate increased linearly with flow speed, and the flame went out (quenching extinction) when the flow was reduced to about 1 cm/s.
findings.conditions: Thin cotton-fiberglass fabric; ISS
findings.safety_implication: Turning off ventilation can starve and extinguish some fires.
findings.score_reason: Gives a concrete, actionable response.

source.title: Flammability Aspects of Fabric in Opposed and Concurrent Air Flow in Microgravity (Ferkul et al., 8th US National Combustion Meeting, 2013; PSI-26)

findings.finding: In microgravity with forced flow, a flame spread steadily against the airflow (opposed flow), while in normal gravity the same downward/opposed configuration self-extinguishes.
findings.conditions: ~10 cm/s flow; thin fabric
findings.safety_implication: Some materials are more flammable in space than Earth tests suggest.
findings.score_reason: Shows enhanced flammability in microgravity.

source.title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment (Ferkul et al., 2013)
source.location: Slide 'Comparison of 0-g and 1-g Opposed Flow Flames'

findings.finding: At about 10 cm/s, concurrent flame spread (2.55 mm/s) was about twice as fast as opposed flame spread (1.21 mm/s).
findings.conditions: Thin fabric; ISS
findings.safety_implication: A fire grows fastest downstream of the airflow; detectors and crew response should focus downstream.
findings.score_reason: Useful number for the chart; narrower applicability.

source.title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment (Ferkul et al., 2013)
source.location: Slide 'Concurrent and Opposed Spread at ~10 cm/s'

findings.finding: Ultem 1000 film and Nomex HT90-40 fabric did not burn in ISS air (21-22% O2) at flow speeds around 15 cm/s; a Nomex-III sample did burn at 22% O2 and 14 cm/s.
findings.conditions: 2 cm wide samples; ISS atmosphere
findings.safety_implication: Fire-retardant materials differ; Nomex-III is less safe than Nomex HT90-40 at cabin oxygen levels.
findings.score_reason: Direct material selection guidance.

source.title: Thickness and Fuel Preheating Effects on Material Flammability in Microgravity from the BASS Experiment (Ferkul et al., 2013)

findings.finding: With oxygen reduced from 21% to 17%, flames over a PMMA (acrylic) sphere stayed blue longer, meaning soot formation was delayed.
findings.conditions: 2 cm PMMA sphere; 12 cm/s flow; nitrogen-diluted air
findings.safety_implication: Lower oxygen changes flame appearance, which can affect optical fire detection.
findings.score_reason: Mainly scientific/model validation value.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: Materials are easier to ignite in low gravity because there is less natural convective cooling of the fuel surface.
findings.conditions: Low-flow microgravity or partial gravity
findings.safety_implication: Overheated surfaces (electronics, heaters) are a bigger ignition risk in space.
findings.score_reason: Relevant to ignition prevention.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: At low flow speeds, flames can spread upstream into the oncoming airflow, the opposite of normal gravity where flames spread downstream with buoyant flow.
findings.conditions: Thin fuel ignited mid-sample; low forced flow
findings.safety_implication: Fire can move in unexpected directions; Earth-based assumptions about fire direction do not hold.
findings.score_reason: Changes how crews anticipate fire movement.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: Radiant heat strongly affects flammability: surface radiative heat loss reduces flammability, but an external radiative heat flux can make materials ignite and spread faster.
findings.conditions: Microgravity solid-fuel tests
findings.safety_implication: Nearby hot surfaces or an existing fire can make other materials ignite more easily.
findings.score_reason: Important but qualitative.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: The flammability limit of liquid fuels with inert-gas suppressants is lower in reduced gravity, so terrestrial standards for inert-gas suppressants do not give the same safety margin in low gravity.
findings.conditions: Heptane and methanol droplets in O2/N2 mixed with CO2, He or Xe; ISS Combustion Integrated Rack
findings.safety_implication: Suppressant concentrations designed on Earth may be insufficient in space.
findings.score_reason: Directly affects fire suppression system design.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: After the visible flame went out, some droplets continued burning as an invisible 'cool flame' before final extinction.
findings.conditions: Large heptane droplets; ISS
findings.safety_implication: A fire can look extinguished while still reacting; crews and sensors should confirm full extinction.
findings.score_reason: Hidden-hazard insight unique to microgravity research.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: Objective: extend FLEX to fuel mixtures, real fuel surrogates, soot formation, slow convective flow effects and droplet-droplet interactions.
findings.conditions: Droplet combustion on ISS
findings.safety_implication: Improves models of how practical liquid fuels burn and go out in space.
findings.score_reason: Objective statement; no safety result extracted yet.

source.title: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA ISS Program Science Office, 2015)

findings.finding: For the materials tested (cellulose, Kapton, silicone rubber, Teflon), a substantial portion of the smoke particles from overheating was below 500 nm in diameter.
findings.conditions: Samples heated below ignition (pre-fire overheat); ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox, Expedition 15
findings.safety_implication: Smoke detectors must be sensitive to very small particles; ionization-type detection handles sub-micron smoke better.
findings.score_reason: Sets design requirements for spacecraft smoke detectors.

source.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) Final Report (Urban et al., 2010; PSI-102)
source.file: SAME Final Science report  03 18 10 with papers attached.pdf

findings.finding: Smoke transport in microgravity is dominated by mixing, so detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity.
findings.conditions: Smoke transport model based on SAME data
findings.safety_implication: Fires may be detected later in space; detectors should be placed close to likely sources and in the ventilation path.
findings.score_reason: Directly affects detection timing and placement.

source.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) Final Report (Urban et al., 2010; PSI-102)
source.file: SAME Final Science report  03 18 10 with papers attached.pdf

findings.finding: Credible pre-fire overheat events can produce broad smoke particle size distributions; detectors that measure more than one property (moment) of the size distribution may perform better.
findings.conditions: Combined SAME and Comparative Soot Diagnostics results
findings.safety_implication: Next-generation spacecraft detectors should use more than one sensing principle.
findings.score_reason: Design recommendation from the researchers.

source.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) Final Report (Urban et al., 2010; PSI-102)
source.file: SAME Final Science report  03 18 10 with papers attached.pdf

findings.finding: Hypothesis tested: without buoyancy, smoke particles grow larger than on Earth, which could cause some smoke detectors not to alarm.
findings.conditions: 66 test points on ISS, July-September 2010, including Pyrell fire-retardant foam
findings.safety_implication: If confirmed, current detector technology may miss some spacecraft smoke.
findings.score_reason: High relevance, but this is the hypothesis; final results are in the SAME-R Final Report (not yet in the dataset).

source.title: PSI-101 SAME-R investigation page (NASA PSI), DOI 10.60555/2np7-jv14

findings.finding: Water-mist portable fire extinguishers were developed for spaceflight; the first two of nine were sent to the ISS in December 2015 to replace CO2 units.
findings.conditions: ISS fire response equipment
findings.safety_implication: Shows how research results are turning into new crew fire response hardware.
findings.score_reason: Operational context rather than an experimental result.
